reader.title: Bloodhound pursuit and hanging near Birmingham (Detroit Free Press sketch)
bases: A1 narrates a fugitive Black man captured by train passengers, then hanged and shot by a party of horsemen who had pursued him with hounds, on an accusation of assault.

As narrated in A1, 'seven or eight men' hanged the man while a dozen bullets were fired, with no officer or legal process, because he was said to have assaulted a white woman; the account is an undated, unnamed first-person sketch reprinted in a miscellany column, so the incident itself cannot be confirmed.
Only A1, a reprint of an unlocated Detroit Free Press sketch, describes the incident; no news report, name, date or follow-up was found.

summary.text: The bloodhound pursuit and hanging near Birmingham is an incident described in a first-person sketch from the Detroit Free Press, reprinted in April 1888, in which an unnamed Black man was run down by hounds, hanged from a tree limb and shot beside a railroad siding.
The leader of the party that killed him said only that he had assaulted a white woman near Birmingham; the sketch gives no date, name or state.
According to the narrator, a passenger train had pulled onto a siding in dense woods to wait out an accident up the line, and the nearest house was a switchman's cabin.
While passengers sat smoking by the track, one man heard the baying of a bloodhound, drew his revolver and had the others spread out in a line a quarter of a mile long.
Within minutes a Black man in torn clothes, with blood on his face and hands, ran into the line and raised his hands when men covered him with revolvers.
Three hounds and then a dozen horsemen arrived, and with hardly a word spoken a rope was thrown over a limb.
Seven or eight men hauled the man up until his toes were two feet off the ground, and a dozen bullets were fired into his body.
As the party left, its leader gave the reason as "Assaulted a white woman near Birmingham."
No report of an inquest, an identification of the dead man or any arrest appears in the coverage.

The Canton Register of Canton, Illinois, printed the piece on April 12, 1888, under the headline "Pursued by Bloodhounds and Hanged by a Mob," in a page-eight miscellany between jokes credited to other papers.

The narrator accepted the leader's one-line accusation as sufficient, writing "That was all, but that was enough," and added that even if all present had been officers of the law, no one would have intervened.
No local news account, wire dispatch or follow-up naming the man or fixing the place was found, so whether the sketch describes a single real incident cannot be established from the coverage.

accounts.label: Passenger's first-person sketch (Detroit Free Press)
accounts.gist: Delayed passengers, alerted by hounds, captured a fleeing Black man; horsemen arrived, hanged him and fired a dozen bullets into him, the leader saying he had assaulted a white woman near Birmingham.

framing.detail: Headline 'Pursued by Bloodhounds and Hanged by a Mob'; the narrator relays the leader's accusation as sufficient ('That was all, but that was enough') and says no one, even officers, would have intervened.

record_check.dossier: Birmingham is named only as where the alleged assault occurred; the hanging took place at an unnamed railroad siding in the woods.
No state is given; Alabama is not stated.
A party of a dozen horsemen with hounds, aided by train passengers; the headline calls it a mob. No lawful authority is mentioned.
The narrative meets every element (killed, illegal, 3+, accusation pretext); probable lynching, with doubt only about whether the sketch reports a real incident.

record_check.record: Passengers ... pursued a Black man with bloodhounds, captured him, hanged him
record_check.dossier: Passengers captured him; the hounds and horsemen were a separate pursuing party, and 'seven or eight men' hanged him.

info: Not given; the sketch is undated. It ran in the Canton Register on 1888-04-12, credited to the Detroit Free Press.

Woods beside a railroad siding where a passenger train waited after an accident up the road; the only house within two miles was a switchman's cabin. Birmingham is named only as the place of the alleged assault ('near Birmingham').
One unnamed 'stalwart black man', clothes torn, blood on face and hands.
Said by the leader of the pursuing party to have 'assaulted a white woman near Birmingham'.

Train passengers formed a line and captured him at revolver point; a dozen horsemen following three hounds arrived; the hanging was done by 'seven or eight men' under a 'leader of the party'. Headline calls them a mob.

sources.note: Miscellany-column reprint credited to the Detroit Free Press: first-person account by a train passenger of a Black man run down by bloodhounds, hanged from a limb and shot; leader says he 'assaulted a white woman near Birmingham'. No date, name or state.
quotes: as seven or eight men ran him up until his toes were two feet above the earth a dozen bullets were fired into his body.
explained the leader of the party as his crowd was ready to go.
